p: Chainsaws do not usually fail all at once. They get harder to start, lose a bit of power, smoke a bit more and start to stall. Most of the time, the cause is a set of cheap wear parts: a dirty air filter, a clogged fuel filter or a tired spark plug. A Husqvarna maintenance kit puts those parts together in one package for your saw.

The 445 and 450 are popular saws with landowners and part-time cutters, and many of them get used hard during storm season and firewood time, then sit for months. A once-a-season tune-up keeps them ready for the next time you need them.

body.h: What to do with the kit
p: Start with a cool saw on a clean bench. Clean the outside of the saw, especially around the air filter cover and the fuel cap. Replace the air filter, remove and replace the spark plug, gapped to the figure in your manual, and fish out the fuel filter from the tank to replace it. Check the fuel line for cracks while you are there.

Then look at the rest of the saw. Clean the cooling fins and the starter area, check the bar rails, sprocket and chain, and make sure the chain brake works. Fill with fresh fuel and bar oil and run it through a few cuts.

Keep a simple log of when you did each tune-up. A strip of tape inside the saw case with the date is enough. It is easy to lose track of when you last changed filters, especially if the saw only runs a few weeks a year.

body.h: Signs your saw needs a tune-up
p: Hard starting, rough idle, bogging under load, loss of power or excessive smoke are all reasons to service the saw. Many people search for a husqvarna chainsaw tune-up kit after a saw that ran well last fall will not start this spring. Old fuel is often part of the problem, so drain old fuel before you start.
If a new plug, filters and fresh fuel do not fix it, the saw may need carburetor or other service. Take it to a qualified shop.
Using fresh fuel and running the carburetor dry before storage prevents most of these problems in the first place. Pre-mixed fuel is a good choice for saws that sit for long stretches between uses.

name: NGK BPMR8Y Spark Plug
title: NGK BPMR8Y Spark Plug: Specs, Cross Reference & Tips
meta: NGK BPMR8Y, the resistor version of the NGK BPM8Y spark plug. Thread and hex size, heat range, cross reference tips and how to install it properly.
tagline: A 14 mm resistor plug in a colder heat range for chainsaws and small engines.
summary: The NGK BPMR8Y is a 14 mm resistor spark plug with a projected tip and a heat range of 8, and it is the resistor version of the NGK BPM8Y spark plug. It is used in a range of chainsaws and small two-stroke engines that call for a slightly colder plug than the BPMR7A.
highlights: 14 mm thread, 13/16 in (20.8 mm) hex
Resistor type, the R version of the BPM8Y
Heat range 8, one step colder than a 7
Projected insulator tip
Common in chainsaws and small two-stroke engines

p: The only letter that separates the bpmr8y from the BPM8Y is the R, which stands for resistor. A resistor plug reduces electrical noise from the ignition system. Many modern engines with electronic ignition specify a resistor plug, and some older engines were designed around the non-resistor version.

If your manual lists the BPMR8Y, use it. If it lists the BPM8Y, check whether the resistor version is an approved substitute before swapping. In practice, many people looking for an ngk bpmr8y spark plug are replacing a BPM8Y and want to know whether it will work. The answer depends on your engine's ignition, so the manual is the final word.

The BPMR8Y is found in a range of chainsaws and other small two-stroke engines. Because several brands of equipment use it, it is a plug many shops keep in stock, and it is worth keeping a couple in the truck if your saws call for it.

In NGK's numbering, a higher number means a colder plug. An 8 runs cooler than a 7, which can suit engines that run hot or at high load. The wrong heat range causes problems: too hot can lead to pre-ignition and engine damage, too cold can lead to fouling.

Searches for bpmr8y cross reference usually come from people matching other brands' plugs. Cross-reference charts are helpful, but heat ranges do not always map exactly between brands. Use the plug the engine maker specifies, or ask a trusted dealer.

Do not change heat range to fix a running problem. If a plug keeps fouling or looks overheated, the cause is usually fuel mix, carburetor tuning, an air leak or a dirty filter. Fix the cause and keep the specified plug.

Check the gap with a wire gauge against your manual before installing. Thread the plug in by hand to avoid cross-threading, then snug it with a plug wrench. Do not over-tighten, especially in aluminum heads. Push the plug boot on until it clicks or seats fully. Always replace a plug with the engine cool and the plug wire or boot removed, and never test for spark by holding the plug near the open spark plug hole. Fuel vapor can ignite.

Read the old plug when it comes out. A dry, light tan or gray color is normal. Wet, black or oily deposits suggest a rich mixture, oil problem or dirty air filter. White or blistered electrodes suggest a lean condition that needs attention.

Spark plugs are cheap and easy to swap, and a fresh plug fixes a lot of starting problems. Keep spares in their packaging in the saw box along with spare filters. If your engine uses the hotter 7 heat range, see the NGK BPMR7A. For other parts, browse power equipment parts.

faq.q: Can I use a BPMR8Y instead of a BPM8Y?
faq.a: Often, but not always. The BPMR8Y adds a resistor. Check your engine's manual or ask a dealer before swapping.

faq.q: What is the heat range of the BPMR8Y?
faq.a: It is an 8 on NGK's scale, one step colder than a 7.

faq.q: What thread size is the BPMR8Y?
faq.a: It has a 14 mm thread and a 13/16 in (20.8 mm) hex.

1/2 in (12.7 mm) reach
Resistor type

p: The ngk cmr7h follows NGK's compact plug naming. C is a 10 mm thread with a 16 mm hex. M marks the compact design for small engines. R means resistor. The 7 is the heat range, and H indicates a 1/2 in (12.7 mm) reach.

Compact plugs are made for small cylinder heads where a full-size plug will not fit. The cmr7h spark plug shows up in trimmers, blowers, edgers, pole saws and small chainsaws, as well as some small four-stroke handheld engines.

Plenty of crews run several brands of small engines, so the same plug may turn up in a trimmer, a blower and a pole saw on the same truck. That makes the CMR7H one of the handier plugs to keep stocked, as long as each machine actually calls for it.

These two plugs look the same and fit the same holes, but they are different heat ranges. In NGK's system, a higher number means a colder plug. The CMR7H is one step colder than the CMR6H. Engines that run hotter or at sustained high load may call for the colder plug.

Only swap between them if your manual lists both. A plug that is too hot for the engine can cause pre-ignition and engine damage, while a plug that is too cold can foul. If you are not sure, match the plug that came out of the engine and confirm it against the manual. See the NGK CMR6H for the hotter version.

Small threads strip easily, especially in aluminum heads. Thread the plug in by hand first and only use the 5/8 in plug wrench for the final snugging. Check the gap with a wire gauge against your manual, and make sure the boot is seated fully on the terminal. Always replace a plug with the engine cool and the plug wire or boot removed, and never test for spark by holding the plug near the open spark plug hole. Fuel vapor can ignite.

When you pull the old plug, look at its color and deposits. Heavy black carbon can mean a rich mixture or dirty air filter. Oily deposits can point to too much oil in the mix. A light tan or gray tip usually means the engine is running well.
Keep spare plugs in their packaging until you use them, so the gap stays where it was set and the electrode does not get damaged in a tool bag.

Replace the plug at the interval in your manual, or any time the engine is hard to start, idles roughly or loses power. A worn or fouled plug is cheap to replace and is one of the first things to check. Keep a few spares in the truck with your other power equipment parts.

faq.q: What is the difference between the CMR7H and CMR6H?
faq.a: They are the same size, but the CMR7H is one heat range colder. Use the one your engine's manual specifies.

faq.q: What thread size is the NGK CMR7H?
faq.a: It has a 10 mm thread, a 5/8 in (16 mm) hex and a 1/2 in (12.7 mm) reach.

faq.q: Is the CMR7H a resistor plug?
faq.a: Yes. The R in the code means it has a built-in resistor.

body.h: Why a tree crew might need one
p: Tree and landscape work does not always stop at the soil line. Crews sometimes need to cut out a section of concrete or pavers to reach roots, trim a curb that a root has lifted, or cut materials for a landscape bed. A power cutter with a diamond wheel like the Husqvarna Vari-Cut S45 handles those jobs.
The S45 sits in Husqvarna's Vari-Cut range as a general-purpose blade. It is meant for users who cut a mix of materials occasionally rather than specialists cutting one material all day.

If you only need to make a few cuts a year, renting a power cutter and buying a suitable blade may make more sense than owning the machine. If your crew does hardscape work regularly, owning a cutter and keeping a general-purpose blade on hand saves trips and rental fees.

body.h: Matching the blade to the saw
p: Diamond blades must match the machine. Check that the blade diameter, arbor size and maximum operating speed all match or exceed what your power cutter requires. Never run a blade on a machine that can spin it faster than its rated maximum speed. Mount it in the correct rotation direction, using the arrow on the blade.
The blade guard must be in place and adjusted correctly. If the blade does not fit the saw properly, do not use it.
Store blades flat or hung in a dry place, away from heavy tools that could bend the core. A blade with a bent core or a damaged arbor hole can wobble and is not safe to use.

Cutting concrete, masonry and stone creates respirable crystalline silica dust, which can cause serious lung disease. OSHA has a specific silica standard for construction. Use wet cutting or approved dust control methods, and wear appropriate respiratory protection as required. Wet cutting also keeps the blade cooler and extends its life.

Wear eye and face protection, hearing protection, gloves and sturdy boots. Keep a firm stance, keep bystanders well back and watch for binding or pinching as the cut progresses. Power cutters can kick back. Only trained operators should use them, following the machine's operator manual.

Let the blade do the work. Forcing it causes overheating and can glaze the segments, which slows cutting. If a blade stops cutting well, it may need dressing by making a few cuts in an abrasive material. Inspect the blade before each use for cracks, missing segments or damage to the core, and replace a damaged blade immediately.
Browse more power equipment parts for other wear items.

Keep track of how much the segments have worn. When the diamond segments are close to the core, the blade is near the end of its life and should be replaced. Never use a blade with cracked or missing segments.

faq.a: Check the diameter, arbor size and maximum speed rating against your saw before using it.

faq.q: Do I need to cut wet?
faq.a: Wet cutting or other approved dust control is strongly recommended to control silica dust, and it extends blade life.

The rod limits movement between the parts, which can reduce stress on a weak union or hold a split together. It is used close to the weakness, while cables installed higher in the crown limit how far the stems can move apart.
Bracing does not make a tree safe on its own. It is one tool in a support system, and it only makes sense when a qualified arborist has assessed the tree and decided the system is appropriate.

Steel cable specifications for tree support systems usually call for EHS strand. If you are installing a tree cabling system, compare this listing with our EHS cable and follow the system design.
Many people looking for cable for sale do not realize there are several grades of galvanized strand. Always check the grade before you buy, and match it to the job.

Common grade cable is useful for non-critical tasks where high strength is not required. Before using any steel cable, check the manufacturer's rated strength for the specific product and diameter, and never use it for lifting, rigging or life support. Tree support systems should be designed and installed by a qualified arborist following ANSI A300 (Part 3) and ANSI Z133, and inspected regularly once installed.
Wear gloves when handling steel strand. Cut ends are sharp, and cable under tension can whip when released.
Store coils dry and off the ground, and keep grades clearly labeled so common grade strand never ends up in a tree support system by mistake.

faq.q: Can I use common grade cable for tree cabling?

Some people search for ehs cord or cable ehs, but the product is the same: extra-high-strength galvanized strand.

The breaking strengths listed in the specs are for EHS strand to ASTM A475. A cabling system is never loaded close to breaking strength. Designs include a large safety margin to allow for dynamic loads, wear and the condition of the wood.

Tree support systems should be designed and installed by a qualified arborist following ANSI A300 (Part 3) and ANSI Z133, and inspected regularly once installed.

faq.q: What does EHS mean on steel cable?

name: 3/8 in Eye Bolt for Tree Cabling
title: 3/8 Eye Bolt for Tree Cabling Hardware
meta: 3/8 eye bolt for tree cabling systems. Where a 3/8 in eye bolt fits, how it pairs with cable and thimbles, and installation and inspection tips.
tagline: A 3/8 in eye bolt for anchoring light cabling systems in trees.
summary: This 3/8 eye bolt is an anchor point for light tree cabling systems, installed through a limb with a washer and nut so a cable can be attached to the eye. It suits smaller limbs and lighter systems where the design calls for 3/8 in hardware.
highlights: 3/8 in diameter eye bolt
Through-bolt anchor for light cabling systems
Pairs with washers, nuts and thimbles
For smaller limbs and lighter system designs
Part of a complete cabling and bracing kit

p: In a steel cabling system, the cable has to attach to the tree at each end. Eye bolts are one of the most common anchors. The bolt goes through a drilled hole in the limb, with a washer and nut on the far side, and the cable attaches to the eye. That spreads the load through the wood and keeps the cable from girdling the limb.

A 3/8 eye bolt is on the lighter end of cabling hardware. It suits smaller limbs and systems where the design calls for 3/8 in hardware. Larger stems and heavier loads call for bigger hardware, so let the system design, not the price, decide the size.

People searching for 3/8 eye bolts are often matching an existing system or replacing worn hardware. When you replace hardware in an existing system, match or exceed the original specification and check the rest of the system while you are in the tree.

When the cable attaches to the eye, a thimble protects the cable from bending too sharply and wearing against the eye. The cable is then terminated with a dead-end grip or other approved method. All parts, including the eye bolt, cable, thimble and termination, need to be rated and sized to work together.

Close or weld the eye as the system design and manufacturer require, so the cable cannot slip out. Use washers sized for the bolt, and do not countersink nuts so deeply that the wood around them is weakened.

Keep a supply of matching washers, nuts and thimbles with your eye bolts so you are never tempted to substitute mismatched hardware in the tree. Store hardware dry to limit corrosion before it is installed.
Tree support systems should be designed and installed by a qualified arborist following ANSI A300 (Part 3) and ANSI Z133, and inspected regularly once installed.

Drill straight, correctly sized holes, aligned with the direction of the cable so the bolt is loaded in line. Avoid drilling through decay or cracks. Tighten the nut so the washer seats firmly against the bark without crushing it. Record the installation and plan regular inspections.

Wear gloves and eye protection when drilling, and use climbing and positioning gear appropriate for work aloft. Drilling and installing hardware while tied in requires the same care as any other work at height.

Inspect cabling systems regularly. Look for wear on the eye and thimble, corrosion, cracks in the wood around the bolt, wood growing over the hardware and changes in cable tension. Replace worn or damaged hardware promptly.

faq.q: What is a 3/8 eye bolt used for in tree cabling?
faq.a: It is a through-bolt anchor for lighter cabling systems. The cable attaches to the eye with a thimble and approved termination.

faq.q: Is a 3/8 in eye bolt strong enough for my tree?
faq.a: It depends on the limb size and system design. A qualified arborist should size hardware following ANSI A300 Part 3.

faq.q: Do I need a thimble with an eye bolt?
faq.a: Yes, a thimble protects the cable where it wraps through the eye and reduces wear.
